articleTitle: Control and analysis of magnetic levitation device based on induced eddy current
abstract: I. INTRODUCTION Magnetic levitation refers to the object using electromagnetic force to overcome gravity and achieve a stable suspension or random equilibrium state without mechanical contact. [1]It is a multidisciplinary comprehensive technology, which is widely used in many emerging industries and other fields. [2]This paper firstly designs the magnetic levitation device composed of field coil, iron core, and aluminum ring. Afterwards the finite element model of magnetic levitation device was set up, and the magnetism-force multi-physical field simulation was conducted where suspension heights of aluminum ring under different coil current of are procured. The experiments based on voltage regulator circuit are conducted, which is compared with simulation results. Finally, the negative feedback is added to the control system, which makes the control of the aluminum ring height more accurate. II. MAGNETIC LEVITATION PRINCIPLE AND SYSTEM ANALYSIS In this paper, as shown in Fig. 1(a), we wrap the wire around the coil frame to be the solenoid coil. When the i<sub xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">1</sub> is changed, the alternating magnetic field generated by the current makes the flux of the aluminum ring which is placed above the coil is continuously changing. So the induced eddy current i<sub xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">2</sub> is generated in the aluminum ring when the i<sub xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">1</sub> changes. The eddy current i<sub xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">2</sub> has a certain phase difference with i<sub xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">1</sub>, and produces a magnetic field which is opposite to the direction of the original magnetic field. When the magnetic force is balanced with the gravity of the aluminum ring, the aluminum ring will be suspending above the coil. The iron core in the coil can play an important role in the magnetic field because its μ is large. In order to seek the relationship between the coil current and the suspension height of the aluminum ring, we control the voltage of the coil to change the current. [3]The main circuit topology is shown in Fig. 1(b). The height control of the aluminum ring is based on the voltage regulating circuit [4] which contains bidirectional thyristor. On the basis of the main circuit, we add the control part. Then the overall topology is shown in Fig. 1(c). The control system in the experiment is composed of three parts. The first part is to realize the synchronization of the control signal and the main circuit voltage by means of voltage zero crossing detection which needs to design a simple zero crossing trigger circuit. The second part is to measure the height of the aluminum ring and input the data to DSP, and the error is determined by the difference between the current height and the setting height. The third part is based on the error value. Apply DSP to delaying the output of the control signal, thereby changing conduction angle thyristor, achieving the voltage control in main circuit. Finally, the height of the metal ring can be controlled. The main materials and parameters are as follows: 1) The core is made of soft iron, its diameter is 1.8cm, height of 20cm. 2) The coil is made of Enameling Copper Wire with 0.61 mm diameter. The number of turns is 4600. III. MAGNETIC-FORCE MULTI PHYSICAL FIELDS SIMULATIONS AND ANALYSIS As shown in Fig. 1(d), the simulation model of the magnetic levitation device was developed in the finite element software. The control circuit was built in circuit simulation software. After the simulation of field circuit coupling and the magnetic-force multi physical fields, we can get the suspension height of aluminum ring at different input current. IV. EXPERIMENTS AND RESULTS Experiments: First the experiment of magnetic levitation device without height feedback has been conducted, shown in Fig. 2(a) and the input current was controlled by open loop control circuit, shown in Fig. 2(b). The data of aluminum ring suspension height have been obtained at different current, and also compared with the simulation results. For the accuracy of the height control, the ultrasonic ranging module was adopted in the control system to measure the current height of aluminum ring as the feedback part, as shown in Fig. 2(c). During this experiment, the starting position of the aluminum ring was 0. Then set the target position for 5cm. The change of the height with time has been recorded. Results: As shown in Fig. 2(d), with the lager current RMS of the coil, the suspension height of aluminum ring is also larger, which is the same as the conclusion of the simulation. As shown in Fig. 2(e), with the feedback part, the ring can get to the height of 5cm from 0 in less than 20s. More importantly, when it get higher than 5cm due to inertia, the system would quickly adjust the current to bring it back to 5cm. V. CONCLUSION This paper verifies the effect of the magnetic levitation device which designed in the second chapter through simulation and experiment. The relationship between the coil current and the suspension height of the aluminum ring is analyzed by designing the open-loop control circuit. The experiment results show that by adding the ultrasonic ranging module to achieve a height negative feedback, the precision and stability of the control system has been improved.

articleTitle: Comparison of magnetic characteristics of three ironless BLDC machines
abstract: Due to the advantages of high efficiency, light mass and small volume, the flywheel based on brushless DC (BLDC) motor with ironless stator is widely utilized in the attitude control system of the micro-satellite. Different methods have been developed for the performance evaluation in PM motors, such as magnetic equivalent circuit (MEC), finite element method (FEM) and subdomain (SD) method. However, the availability of fast, accurate, and reliable analytical models is still preferred during the motor initial design. In order to further improve the efficiency and reduce the waveform distortion of back EMF, the magnetic characteristics of three different ironless BLDC motors are compared. The three different types are BLDC motor without back-iron, with back-iron, and with dual-rotor, respectively, as shown in Fig. 1(a). Firstly, the analytical solutions in the three motors are obtained and the magnetic field distributions around the coil region are compared. Secondly, the back-EMF with different combination of pole number and slot number, winding configuration including non-overlapping and overlapping windings are investigated. Thirdly, the copper losses and efficiency are calculated and compared. Finally, the prototype is fabricated and tested to verify the analysis.

articleTitle: Development and evaluation of tip position estimation system of gastric tube for practical applications
abstract: Summary form only given. Introduction For patients who have difficulty swallowing, nasoor oro-gastric tubes are usually used to deliver nutrients to the stomach. However, a gastric tube incorrectly inserted into the lungs instead of the stomach can be fatal. To insert the tube into the stomach correctly, we propose a method to estimate the position of a permanent magnet attached to the tip of the tube by solving the inverse problem using measurement data obtained from several magneto-impedance (MI) sensors placed outside the patient's body [1]. In the practical application, the tip position should be easily determined. With tablet computers becoming more prevalent nowadays, doctors and nurses prefer using them for confirming the position of the tip of the gastric tube. However, a tablet is insufficient for solving the inverse problem. Furthermore, a tablet often has ferromagnetic materials, which may adversely affect its performance. To overcome this problem, we developed a distributed cooperative system for estimating the tube tip position in a LAN setup. In addition, we evaluated whether the presence of ferromagnetic materials near a sensor affects the performance of estimating the tip position. Methods Fig. 1 shows the distributed cooperative system setup used for tip position estimation. A server PC estimates the tip position from the magnetic flux of a permanent magnet b(t) by solving the inverse problem. The details of the inverse algorithm are described in [1]. The estimated position information is sent to a tablet via a wireless LAN. Finally, the tablet displays the position. To reduce the effect of geomagnetism and ferromagnetic materials near the MI sensors, b(t) is estimated by subtracting the measured magnetic flux data without permanent magnet bnoise(t) from that with permanent magnet bmeas(t) as follows: b(t) = bmeas(t) - <; bnoise(t)> (1) The distance between the MI sensors and the tablet is approximately 65 mm. We used a permanent magnet with a diameter of 5 mm and a length of 15 mm for evaluating the estimation performance. The permanent magnet was moved using three-axis motorized stages. Results Fig. 2 shows the results of the tip position estimation error on the x-y plane when the distance between the sensor plane and the permanent magnet z is 90, 110, 130, and 150 mm. As shown, the error distribution does not change whether or not the tablet is placed near the MI sensors. This indicates that the effect of ferromagnetic materials in the tablet can be effectively reduced by using (1). The mean of the tip position estimation error is less than 10 mm even when the tablet is placed near the MI sensors and z = 150 mm, thus meeting the requirement in the real clinical application. The calculation time of the inverse problem is less than 0.20 s, and the tip position could be displayed on the tablet every 0.25 s, facilitating the observation of the tip position in real time.

articleTitle: 2D semi-analytical modeling of eddy currents in multiple non-connected conducting segments
abstract: To model parasitic forces and power losses due to eddy currents in electromagnetic devices, several techniques can be used. In this paper, the 2D Fourier analysis technique from is extended to analytically model eddy currents in multiple non-connected conductive segments. The forces on conducting parts due to induced eddy currents and the power losses are calculated using the developed method and compared to FE results.

articleTitle: Analysis of a novel linear doubly salient slot permanent magnet motor
abstract: Over the past few decade, several novel linear motor topologies including switched reluctance linear motor (SRLM) and doubly salient linear motor (DSLM) have been extensively researched for long distance direct drive applications due to the increasing demand of low cost, low PM consumption and simple structure.However, these motors still suffer from unavoidable cogging force and high force ripple even if adopting end assistant teeth, so that they requires additional control algorithms to compensate in high precision applications. Moreover, the excitation of SRLM remains unipolar which causes magnetic noise and vibration in these motors. In order to solve these problems, a novel linear doubly salient slot permanent magnet motor (LDSSPMM) is proposed. It has doubly salient primary and secondary structures with PMs inserted in the primary slots, which exhibits some significant advantages. Because the PM flux is only located in the primary at open circuit, LDSSPMM has negligible cogging force and end effect which simplifies the optimal design. It is also low PM consumption with both PMs and windings on the primary, especially beneficial to long stroke. Moreover, it can protect the control system at fault condition of high speed flux-weakening due to the PM flux is only shorted in the primary when armature current is zero.

In the first method, we detect small changes in the largest projection of coupled magnetic moment (Δmz) as the material is driven into resonance. The second method measures the change in Δm<sub xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">z</sub> caused by the resonance induced thermal heating.

articleTitle: Analysis of the hyperthermia efficiency and MRI quality trade off in PMMA-based bone cements loaded with magnetic nanoparticles
abstract: Summary form only given. In this work, T<sub xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">1</sub>-weighted images (MP-RAGE sequence) of cylindrical PMMA mixed with MNP (PMMA-MNP) samples have been carried out in agar gel phantoms with a Siemens 3T MR scanner. Two types of MNP were tested (iron oxide powder and ferrofluid suspension) with different concentrations. For every MRI session, 21 slices were selected centralized around the half length of the sample. The artifact caused by the magnetic nanoparticles was measured in each slice by fitting an ellipse to the disturbed area and subtracting the radius of the sample from the average of the major and minor ellipse radii. As a tool for the fitting, the images were masked with a threshold of 30% of their maximal value. Since each phantom was measured twice, this procedure led to a total of 42 values, indicating the spread of the artifact, for each MNP concentration. Boxplots of the measured artifact as function of MNP concentrations were depicted. Ferrofluid samples give rise to lower MRI artifacts compared to samples prepared with the iron oxide powder and having the same MNP concentration. Moreover, the values vary less between the slices for ferrofluid samples as can be seen by smaller interquartile ranges. Results demonstrate that both concentration and type of MNP affect the MRI behavior of PMMA-MNP samples. In this study, we provide a balance of the needed MNP concentration to have an efficient magnetic hyperthermia treatment with minimum artifact for the required quality of MRI in case of PMMA-based bone cements loaded with MNP.

articleTitle: Stability diagram of perpendicular magnetic tunnel junction with a composite free layer
abstract: Magnetic tunnel junctions (MTJs) have become a basic building block for various types of spintronics devices, such as magnetic random access memory (MRAM) cells, magnetic field sensors and microwave generators or detectors. There are a few ways to realize perpendicularly magnetized MTJ, which are characterized by greater thermal stability than their in-plane magnetized counterparts. Taking advantage of the interface anisotropy yields the best results, especially in terms of high tunnel magnetoresistance (TMR) measured typically in MTJs with CoFeB/MgO/CoFeB trilayer. Recent studies on perpendicular MTJ resulted in the TMR ratio exceeding 200 % [1] thanks to careful optimization of both the free layer (FL) and reference layer (RL) structure. We report on the perpendicular MTJ with a composite CoFeB/W/CoFeB FL [2,3] which is characterized by high perpendicular magnetic anisotropy and spin polarization resulting in up to 180 % TMR measured at room temperature and above 280 % TMR at low temperature. The multilayers with the following structure were deposited: buffer / SyF / spacer / CoFeB(1) / MgO(1.2) / CoFeB(t<sub xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">FL</sub>) / W(0.3) / CoFeB(0.5) / MgO(1) / capping (thicknesses in nm), with t<sub xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">FL</sub> ranging from 1 up to 1.6 nm and RA product equal to 10 Ωμm<sup xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">2</sup>. For the 1.5 nm thick CoFeB sublayer, the TMR of 180 % at room temperature and 280 % at 20 K was measured. The stability diagram was modeled based on Ref. [4]. Additionally, it was assumed that in-plane all (out-of-plane al) torque component scales linearly (quadratically) with the applied current [5]. To account for additional physical effects that contribute to the stability diagram, namely VCMA and temperature effect, the coercive field HC is scaled by the factor: HC = HK(1-V<sub xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">K</sub>V-(T/ kT)1/2) where V is the applied voltage, HK is the anisotropy field, V<sub xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">K</sub> is the VCMA coefficient and Ta is the ambient temperature. kT represents the dependence of the temperature on the coercive field. The damping factor was measured independently by the broadband FMR technique. An increase of the TMR from 140% for t<sub xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">FL</sub> = 1.1 nm up to TMR = 180% for t<sub xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">FL</sub> = 1.5 nm is explained by an increase of the spin polarization for thicker ferromagnetic layer. A rapid reduction of the TMR for t<sub xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">FL</sub> = 1.6 nm is caused by the transition of the FL magnetization vector to the sample plane. Electronic transport properties were measured in perpendicular magnetic field (see Fig. 1). It has been already established that apart from the conventional STT effect in MTJs with a relatively thin MgO barrier, the switching process can be also affected by the VCMA effect in a thin FL. To investigate the switching process in more detail, we repeated the R(V) loops measurement, with different constant magnetic field. The stability diagram was obtained in this way both at low (T = 20 K) and room temperature (T = 300 K) for the MTJ with t<sub xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">FL</sub> = 1.1 nm. The 300 K result is presented in Fig. 2. The diagram was modelled using STT, VCMA and thermal effects taken into account. In addition, for the precise derivation of the STT coefficients, the magnetization damping was calculated based on an independent FMR measurement. Fitting the experimental stability diagram to the model yielded the temperature coefficients of kT = 0.0014 T/K. This parameter was kept constant for MTJs with different t<sub xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">FL</sub>. Remaining parameters of the stability diagrams for each t<sub xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">FL</sub> were modeled independently. For t<sub xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">FL</sub> = 1.1 nm, the following STT components were obtained: all = 0.024 T/V and al = 0.02 T/V, however, we note that the modeled stability diagram is insensitive to al, which agrees with another macrospin approach based on Landau-Lifshitz-Gilbert equation presented in Ref. [6]. In-plane torque τll was thereafter recalculated and as the result we obtained τll = 4.5*10<sup xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">-19</sup> Nm/V, which agrees well with literature values of STT in the case of an in-plane MTJ [5,7]. Regarding VCMA, the best results for MTJ with t<sub xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">FL</sub> = 1.1 nm were obtained for V<sub xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">K</sub> = 0.14 1/V. Based on the following relation: V<sub xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">K</sub> = κ/μ<sub xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">0</sub>H<sub xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">C</sub>M<sub xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">S</sub>t<sub xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">FL</sub>t<sub xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">B</sub>, where t<sub xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">B</sub> = 1.2 nm is the tunnel barrier thickness, VCMA coeficient of κ = 77 fJ/ Vm was calculated, which fits well commonly measured values for CoFeB/ MgO devices [3,8]. The project is supported by Polish National Center for Research and Development grant No. LIDER/467/L-6/14/NCBR/2015 and grant Preludium UMO-2015/17/N/ST3/02276 from National Science Center, Poland.

articleTitle: The study of Fe83Ga17 films act as magnetostrictive actuator on PZT substrate
abstract: Summary form only given. We are investigating the properties of Fe-Ga films on PZT substrate. In the Fe-Ga/PZT magnetoelectric devices the Fe-Ga magnetostrictive films act as a driver, therefore it should exhibit good magnetic and electrical and mechanical properties. During sputtering, Ar pressure was changed and we obtained corresponding Fe-Ga films. It is shown that there is a strong relation between the gas pressure and adherence, conductivity, magnetic and mechanical properties of Fe-Ga thin films. We found the Fe-Ga/PZT devices with highest Young's modulus also performance best in the magnetoelectric coupling test, the ME coefficient was 0.17 V/cm Oe, although the thickness of Fe-Ga film only about 300 nm. The saturation magnetization of thin films decreased significantly and the saturation magnetic field increases. When the sputtering pressure increased, collision frequency between sputtered Fe-Ga atom and Ar+ also increases, which resulted in the atomic energy of Fe-Ga deposited on the substrate decreased, so the diffusing capacity and the quality of crystallization became worse. Meanwhile grain boundary and defects increased, so the scattering of electron transport processes is intensified, that is the reason why the resistivity of the film increase with the sputtering pressure. Also high pressure made the defects and the stress among grains and interface, which inhibited the rotation of the magnetic domains and films show poor soft magnetic properties. And the domain structure of FeGa films on PZT was dendritic.

abstract: Summary form only given. In this paper we investigate the structural and magnetic properties of Fe<sub xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">1-x</sub>Ga<sub xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">x</sub> alloys (x = 0.0 - 0.30) posessing the A2, D0<sub xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">3</sub>, and L1<sub xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">2</sub> structures by means of the density functional theory. The ground state calculations were carried out by using the Spin-Polarized Relativistic Korringa-Kohn-Rostoker (SPR-KKR) code and relativistic hamiltonian (REL) [6]. The exchange correlation energy was taken into account in the formulation of Perdew, Burke and Ernzerhof (PBE) implemented in the general gradient approximation. The calculations of opti- mized lattice parameters were carried for compositions with x = 0 up to 0.3. The obtained equilibrium lattice parameters were further used to calculate the magnetocrystalline anisotropy and magnetic exchange constants for crystal lattices studied.

articleTitle: A double-negative waveguide metacomposite enabled by ferromagnetic microwires
abstract: Summary form only given. Metamaterials have aroused tremendous interests in recent years owing to their peculiar electromagnetic (EM) properties and fascinating potential applications. For conventional metamaterials, these exciting properties are generally realised from their periodical structure and thus are usually detached to materials properties of internal building blocks. Also, the considerable manufacturing costs are the other factor that restricts metamaterials for mass production. A term of `metacomposites' has been previously proposed and its definition is threefold.(I) A metacomposite is a piece of metamaterial characterised by a double-negative (DNG) feature, i.e., a negative permittivity and a negative permeability. (II) The final EM properties of metacomposites are somewhat dependent on the fillers' intrinsic materials properties. (III) Metacomposites can be manufactured and tailored via an easy engineering technique to promise their cost-effectiveness. Ferromagnetic microwires are acknowledged as feasible building blocks to construct metamaterials most recently arising from their excellent soft magnetic properties and flexible magnetic tunability. In this work,a more controllable waveguide technique to model and study microwire-metacomposites and demonstrate remarkable metamaterial behaviour at microwave frequencies was deployed.

articleTitle: Interplay between epitaxial strain and low dimensionality effects in a ferrimagnetic oxide
abstract: Thin film properties are strongly influenced by strain and low dimensionality effects, especially when the film thickness is about a few unit cells, which corresponds to the thicknesses targeted in most of contemporary studies. In oxides, these effects are responsible for the dramatic modification of the physical properties that sometimes can change the nature of a material. Nevertheless, it is not always possible to distinguish the contribution of the strain to the changes in physical properties from the contribution due to low dimensional effects. In the present study, bismuth iron garnet Bi<sub xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">3</sub>Fe<sub xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">5</sub>O<sub xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">12</sub> (BIG) is chosen to separate both effects. This material possesses, among other outstanding physical properties (including magnetoelectricity), the giant Faraday rotation that allows to investigate films with the thickness below a few unit cells. Three series of BIG films of various thicknesses were grown on three isostructural substrates with different lattice parameters: Y<sub xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">3</sub>Al<sub xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">5</sub>O<sub xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">12</sub>(001), Gd<sub xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">3</sub>Ga<sub xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">5</sub>O<sub xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">12</sub>(001) and (GdCa)<sub xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">3</sub>(GaMgZr)<sub xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">5</sub>O<sub xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">12</sub>(001). The structural, magnetic and magneto-optic properties were studied as a function of film thickness and strain. Advanced scanning transmission electron microscopy measurements allowed to evidence different relaxation mechanisms of the films. Furthermore, critical behavior of the BIG films was investigated in the vicinity of the Curie temperature. The obtained results allowed to distinguish between the low dimensional effects and the strain due to the epitaxial growth. While the size reduction is mostly responsible for the decrease of the magnetic characteristics of the films, the strain influences rather the critical thickness below which the material starts to behave as a low dimensional system.

articleTitle: All-optical switching behaviours in synthetic ferrimagnetic heterostructures with different ferromagnetic-layer Curie temperatures
abstract: Summary form only given. All-optical switching (AOS) has been observed in ferromagnetic (FM) layers and synthetic ferrimagnetic heterostructures [1-4]. In this work, we use anomalous Hall effect (AHE) measurements to demonstrate controlled helicity-dependent switching in synthetic ferrimagnetic heterostructures. The two FM layers are engineered to have different Curie temperatures Tc1 (fixed) and Tc2 (variable). We show that irrespective of whether Tc2 is higher or lower than Tc1, the final magnetic configuration of the heterostructure is controlled by using the laser polarization to set the magnetic state of the FM layer with the highest Tc. All samples were grown on glass substrates at room temperature by DC magnetron sputtering. Two sets of samples were prepared. The first set are single FM layers with layer composition Ta (3 nm)/Pt (4 nm)/FM1(2)/Pt capping (4 nm), where FM1 = Co (0.6 nm) is a Co layer and FM2 = CoFeB (tCoFeB)/Pt(0.4 nm)/ CoFeB (tCoFeB) (0.2 ≤ tCoFeB ≤ 0.6 nm) is a composite CoFeB layer where both CoFeB layers are ferromagnetically coupled and act as a single layer. FM1 and FM2 were used to produce the second set of synthetic ferrimagnetic samples with layer structure Ta (3 nm)/Pt (4 nm)/FM1/Pt (0.4 nm)/Ru (0.9 nm)/Pt (0.4 nm)/FM2/Pt capping (4 nm). The Ru layer provides the antiferromagnetic RKKY interlayer exchange coupling between the adjacent FM1 and FM2 layers while the Pt layers on either side of the Ru layer can tune the strength of the coupling and stabilize their perpendicular anisotropy [5]. To study the AOS, we use a Ti: sapphire fs-laser with a wavelength of 800 nm and a pulse duration of 43 fs. A quarter-wave plate is used to create a circularly polarized [right(σ+) and left-handed (σ-)] beam. We first measured the magnetic properties of the FM1 and FM2 layers using vibrating sample magnetometry (VSM). All FM samples show full remanence in perpendicular hysteresis loops at room temperature (not shown). The temperature-dependent magnetization scans (not shown) give a Curie temperature Tc1 of 524 K for FM1. For FM2, increasing tCoFeB increases its Curie temperatureTc2. At tCoFeB = 0.5 nm, Tc2 - Tc1. Hall crosses are patterned by optical lithography and ion milling. The width of the current carrying wire is - 5 um, giving a DC current density of - 6 x 109 A/m2 during the measurement. Figure 1(a) shows the resulting perpendicular Hall hysteresis loop of the synthetic ferrimagnetic sample with tCoFeB = 0.2 nm. At remanence, the stable magnetic configurations are the two antiparallel orientations of FM1 and FM2 [State I and II in Fig. 1(a)]. To study the AOS, we swept the laser beam with a power of 0.45 mW and a speed of 1 μm/sec across the Hall cross, and the corresponding Hall voltage was constantly monitored. In Fig. 1(b), we show the normalized Hall voltage, VHall, as a function of the laser beam position x for both beam polarizations σ+ and σ-. The initial magnetic configuration was State I. When the beam is at the center of the cross (position B), both beam polarizations give VHall - 0. As the beam leaves the cross (position C), the σbeam changes the magnetic configurations from State I to State II (FM1 magnetization pointing down), while the system reverts to State I using the σ+ beam. Changing the initial configuration from State I to State II results in the same final magnetic configurations, determined by the laser beam polarizations (not shown). Similar results (not shown) were obtained for samples with tCoFeB ≤ 0.4 nm. However, at tCoFeB = 0.6 nm, the σbeam results in the final magnetic configurations with FM2 magnetization pointing down (State I) and the σ+ beam results in the State II configuration, suggesting that the final state is determined by the beam polarization acting on the layer with the highest Tc. Figure 2(a) shows the perpendicular Hall hysteresis loops of the synthetic ferrimagnetic sample with tCoFeB = 0.5 nm (Tc of both FM layers are identical). Similar to the sample with tCoFeB = 0.2 nm, the two antiparallel states are stable at remanence. We performed laser sweeping measurement with State I as the initial magnetic state. In Fig. 2(b), we show the corresponding variation of VHall as a function of x. Similarly, VHall - 0 when the beam is at the center of the cross (position B). However, as the laser beam leaves the cross (position C), both polarizations σ+ and σresult in reverting to the initial magnetic state I. Changing the initial state to State II (not shown) results in reverting to State II after the beam sweep. The final state is independent of the beam polarization and solely determined by the initial state. These results clarify the all-optical switching behaviours in synthetic ferrimagnetic heterostructures, providing a pathway toward opto-spintronics devices made of complex magnetic multilayers and capable of all-optical control of magnetic configurations.

articleTitle: Current controlled domain wall velocity in amorphous microwires
abstract: Summary form only given. Here we report on the effect of a d.c. and a.c. current which passes through cylindrical Fe<sub xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">77.5</sub>Si<sub xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">7.5</sub>B<sub xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">15</sub> and Co<sub xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">68.18</sub>Fe<sub xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">4.32</sub>Si<sub xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">12.5</sub>B<sub xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">15</sub> amorphous microwires on their domain wall velocity.alternating field is considerable lower. In FeSiB glass covered wires that have a high positive magnetostriction that determine a inner core magnetized along the wire and an outer shell radially magnetized, a current passing along the wire cannot induce a domain wall, but will modify significant the value of the domain wall velocity induced by a dc longitudinal magnetic field. In the CoFeSiB glass covered wires having nearly zero magnetostriction, annealed to obtain an inner core axially magnetized and an outer shell circumferentially magnetized, applying an a.c. current along the wire it is possible to induce a domain wall in the outer shell and to control its velocity. These results are essential for the control of domain wall dynamics, with important consequences on the development of magnetic domain wall logic devices and for other applications.

articleTitle: STT-MRAM is moving to large scale commercialization (at last!)
abstract: Summary form only given. MRAM memory technology is now an old memory with a decade passed since the introduction of a first commercial product in 2006 by Freescale, now Everspin, its MRAM spin off company. A decade ago, there was high hopes toward MRAM which was claiming to be the universal memory combining contradictory properties such as non volatility, high speed, high endurance, high density and low power. But reality has been different, and MRAM technology has not catch up as expected, and did not substitute dominant stand alone DRAM and NAND technologies, nor embedded flash or SRAM. The main issue has been poor scalability of MRAM technology compared to incumbent technologies whose products density was increasing by a fast rate of +50% per year. But times are changing : MRAM moved to a more scalable version, STTMRAM, and pace of higher density products for incumbent technologies is slowing down, especially in embedded MCU applications. Also, high speed memory is urgently needed in enterprise storage market driven by exploding network traffic. Thus, we expect STTMRAM commercialization will increase rapidly in the next 3 to 5 years, still in specific markets, before moving to main stream markets targeted by NAND and DRAM. We will introduce in this presentation an overview of memory market, main technologies, main applications and players. Then we will present an overview of emerging Non Volatile Memory under development, and we will focus on STTMRAM : what are the key STTMRAM applications ? who are the key players today and in the future ? Which market forecast do we expect for STTMRAM for the next 5 years ?

articleTitle: 3D new calculation principle of levitation force between permanent magnet and Hard Type-II superconductor using integral approach
abstract: Summary form only given. In this paper, the calculation of the interaction forces between the permanent magnet (PM) and a bulk superconductor (SC) used as a classical levitation system is given. The forces and mutual inductances are developed via Green's functions using Amperian model, assuming a cuboidal thin coil for (PM) and a superposition of closed loops of rectangular cross section of the (SC). In the superconductor, the critical current (J<sub xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">c</sub>) is known, but the variable penetration thickness of J<sub xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">c</sub> is given from external magnetic fields by Bean's critical state model (BCSM). All the analytical results are obtained with a dynamic representation of all penetration thicknesses of Jc depending on of applied external magnetic field variations.

articleTitle: Effect of stress on magnetic properties of annealed glass-coated Co71Fe5B11Si10Cr3 amorphous microwires
abstract: Summary form only given. A considerable amount of interest in the field of applied magnetism has been devoted to investigating amorphous magnetically soft microwires due to their local dimensionality, cost-effective fabrication, interesting soft magnetic properties, large magnetoimpedance (MI) and stress-magnetoimpedance. Thanks to the MI effect, the amorphous wires-based magnetic sensors have opened the avenue for achieving PicoTesla magnetic field sensitivity with low noise at room temperatures. In general, hysteretic magnetic properties of amorphous ferromagnetic microwires were found to be significantly dependent on the magnetostriction coefficient λs, and on the amount of the internal stresses σi, which are induced during solidification and by glass-coating. The internal stress distribution is strongly related to the fabrication method of glass-coated microwires which technically requires rapid solidification of microwire composite from its melt form. Consequently, heat treatment in terms of annealing can be seen as very affective, from the impact point of view, to alter and even enhance soft magnetic properties of low-magnetostrictive microwires. On the other hand, many applications require the use of relatively hard magnetic microwires as biasing elements and to design specific harmonic spectra of the voltage response induced by the wire remagnetization. Such properties can be also achieved by a proper choice of the wire composition and annealing treatment. In the present work, we performed a comprehensive study on the effect of annealing on magnetic properties; hysteresis loop, magnetoimpedance and magnetostriction coefficient of amorphous glasscoated microwires. Additionally, the sensitivity of the magnetic properties to external stresses applied to the annealed wires was investigated. Effect of annealing on glass-coated Co<sub xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">71</sub>Fe<sub xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">5</sub>B<sub xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">11</sub>Si<sub xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">10</sub>Cr<sub xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">3</sub> amorphous wires with small magnetostriction constant is studied in the present work. The annealing process was carried out in a programmable furnace in air atmosphere at temperature Tann = 573K, for different periods of time (30 and 60 minutes). The wires under the study are based on Corich composition according to the stoichiometric formula: Co<sub xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">71</sub>Fe<sub xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">5</sub>B<sub xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">11</sub>Si<sub xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">10</sub>Cr<sub xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">3</sub> with two different diameters: (i) total diameter of 29.5 μm and a core diameter of 23.9 μm and (ii) total diameter of 41.5 μm and a metallic core diameter of 36.3 μm, respectively for the samples labeled (No.1) and (No.2). The Curie temperature (Tc=637 K) and crystallization temperature (Tcr=736 K) were estimated from DSC curves using the standard IT application. The microwire in amorphous state (No.1) with small positive magnetostriction demonstrated a coercivity increase as a result of annealing, which is attributed to enhancement of either magnetostriction constant or axial stress. It is also seen that the external stress effect on the magnetization behavior becomes completely different after annealing. In the case of a wire with partial crystalline structure, annealing did not result in the modifications of the magnetization processes. However, this wire demonstrated enhanced stress sensitivity of the coercivity after annealing as shown in figure 2. It can be clearly observed that the coercivity increased significantly to 284 A/m (around 5.6 times) as a stress of 1.19 GPa was applied. to wire labeled (No.1). Such increase in coercivity with applied stress can be attributed to the occurrence of crystallite texture. Therefore, we can confidently conclude that the annealing process of partially crystalline wire may enhance magnetically bistable behavior. Magneto-elastic anisotropy in amorphous wires may result in complicated domain structure caused by particular internal stress distribution. In the case of partially crystallized wires there is an additional source of the anisotropy which turns out to be also sensitive to the mechanical stress. The nature of this strong stress effect should be further investigated. Our results have indicated the appropriateness of the annealing processing for enhancing the magnetic properties of the wires under investigations to meet specific applications. Precisely, the coercivity increasing against stress promotes wider range of implementations as wireless stress-sensors.

abstract: Summary form only given. All films were deposited by using ultra-high-vacuum magnetron sputtering system. The crystalline structures and magnetic properties were measured by X-ray diffraction (XRD), Vibrating sample magnetometer (VSM), and Superconducting quantum interference device (SQUID), respectively. articleTitle: Spin transport in organic semiconductors: From spin pumping by ferromagnetic resonance to lateral spin-valves
abstract: Summary form only given. Organic semiconductors (OSC) such as conjugated polymers/molecules are enabling flexible, large area optoelectronic devices, such as organic light-emitting diodes, transistors, and solar cells. Due to their exceptionally long spin lifetimes, these carbon-based materials could also have an important impact on spintronics, where carrier spins play a key role in transmitting, processing and storing information. Here, we combine three different approaches to study spin transport in OSC: spin pumping induced by ferromagnetic resonance (FMR), vertical and lateral spin-valves. i) We have recently demonstrated spin pumping by FMR in a ferromagnet (FM)/ conjugated polymer/nonmagnetic (NM) spin-sink trilayer to demonstrate the ability of polarons to carry pure spin currents over hundreds of nanometers with long spin relaxation times of up to a millisecond and to exhibit Hanle precession. Our trilayer architecture relies on spin pumping from a FM material for spin injection into the organic and on the inverse spin-Hall effect (ISHE) in a NM metal with strong spin-orbit coupling for detection of spins transmitted through the organic layer. This technique allows us to measure both spin and charge carrier transport through the organic in the same device. We have also studied spin pumping on different organic materials such as PBTTT, F4TCNQ doped PBTTT as well as P3HT with a thickness dependence in order to characterize the spin diffusion length of the organic layer. ii) We report the results of magnetoresistance (MR) measurements in vertical organic spin-valves where an organic material is contacted by two FM electrodes (Py) with the magnetic field oriented parallel to the layer stack. The organic layer is generally thick enough to avoid any coupling between the two FM electrodes. The MR is measured as a function of temperature, bias and orientation. iii) Finally, we report our attempts at spin injection into OSC using lateral organic spin-valves (LSV). We will present the fabrication method using electron beam lithography and evaporation/sputtering techniques. Typical LSV structures consist of two laterally separated ferromagnetic Co or other ferromagnetic electrodes (with and without tunnel barriers), connected by a patterned OSC ribbon of F4TCNQ doped PBTTT. In these structures, the charge and spin currents can be separated in order to rule out the MR effects of the electrodes and to avoid the presence of a background resistance coming from the contacts. We compared the devices where the FM layer is in direct contact with the organic to the one obtained using tunnel contacts such as FM/MgO and FM/Al<sub xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">2</sub>O<sub xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">3</sub>. These studies are very important in order to optimize the magnetic contacts to organic for future organic-based spintronic devices.

abstract: Summary form only given. The magnetic dead layers in films a few nanometers thick are investigated for La<sub xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">0.7</sub>Sr<sub xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">0.3</sub>MnO<sub xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">3</sub> on SrTiO<sub xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">3</sub> (STO), LaAlO<sub xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">3</sub> (LAO) and (LaAlO<sub xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">3</sub>)(Sr<sub xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">2</sub>TaAlO<sub xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">6</sub>)<sub xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">0.7</sub> (LSAT) substrates. An anomalous moment found to persist above the Curie temperature of the La<sub xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">0.7</sub>Sr<sub xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">0.3</sub>MnO<sub xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">3</sub> films is not attributed to the films, but to oxygen vacancies at or near the surface of the substrate. The contribution to the moment from the substrate is as high as 20 μB /nm<sup xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">2</sup> in the case of STO or LSAT. The effect is increased by adding an STO cap layer. Taking this d-zero magnetism into account, extrapolated magnetic dead layer thicknesses of 0.8 nm, 1.5 nm and 3.0 nm are found for the manganite films grown on LSAT, STO and LAO substrates, respectively. An STO cap layer eliminates the LSMO dead layer.

articleTitle: Assessment of a biocompatible nanovehicle with adjustable magnetic properties
abstract: Summary form only given. In the frame of this work the synthesis of self-assembled magnetic and biocompatible nanovehicles movable in aqueous solutions by a magnetic field is presented. The systems consist of a mesoporous silicon template and encapsulated iron oxide nanostructures, both materials known to be biocompatible. Two routes are applied to produce iron oxide nanostructures embedded within porous silicon (PSi). First, readily synthesized superparamagnetic iron oxide nanoparticles (NPs) are infiltrated into the pores. The second attempt is the chemical deposition of iron oxide structures inside the PSi templates. Concerning the adjustability of the magnetic properties of the system the loading procedure of the PSi with iron oxide NPs will be elucidated in detail as well as the growth of iron oxide structures within the pores. An assessment of the iron oxide deposition dependent on the template and the chemical parameters as well as of the magnetic properties in dependence on the particle size and template morphology of the nanocomposite will be presented. A further approach is the transition from magnetite to the stable hematite phase by heat treatment of the specimens. A sufficient filling leading to a magnetization high enough for the movement of the nanovehicles within aqueous surroundings (e.g. body fluid) by a magnetic field of 0.1 T could be reached easily.

articleTitle: Design and implementation of a low frequency pulsed magnetic field generator applicable to unilateral NMR
abstract: Pulsed magnetic field generation circuits find varied applications inclusive of biological applications [1, 2], magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) [3], transcranial magnetic stimulation (TMS) [4] and magneto-optical switching [5]. In this work, a low field, low frequency (<; 5MHz), pulsed magnetic field generation circuit suited for unilateral nuclear magnetic resonance (NMR) applications is presented. A magnetic flux density of approximately 1000G is generated using an inductive load with a FET-based switch. The inductive load resonates at a frequency of 5MHz which is the precession frequency of <sup xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">1</sup>H protons in a magnetic flux of 1000G. The designed circuit can be tuned to operate at resonant frequencies of other chemical species. In this paper, the design parameters and operation of a prototype pulsed field generator will be discussed.

articleTitle: Magnetic circuit evaluation of conductive and near-field noise suppression using Co-Zr-Nb film
abstract: Less than few-μm magnetic film is proposed a next generation noise suppressor for IC chips at a GHz frequency range. The magnetic films suppress the conductive noise by ferromagnetic resonance (FMR) and Joule losses and also suppress the near-field noise by the eddy current and permeance. However, there are some cases that the magnetic film can increase the near-field intensity at the FMR frequency. These results indicate that the integrated design method is necessary to control noise suppression because the control of the conductive and near-field noise suppression depending on each other. This paper discusses the integrated evaluation and discuss the mechenism of the conductive and near-field noise suppression using magnetic circuit network for the integrated design.

abstract: Permanent magnet (PM) machines have been widely applied over the past few decades, such as renewable power generation, electric vehicles, domestic appliances, etc. This paper proposes a double superposition method to fast and accurately predict the cogging torque of PM machines with axial-varying rotor eccentricities. The original axial-varying eccentric machine is cut into N uniform slices along the axial direction and each slice is considered to be axial-even. Due to the axial-varying characteristic, each slice will have different eccentricity magnitude.

abstract: Weyl semimetals have emerged as the three-dimensional counterpart of graphene with linear energy dispersion along all three directions. articleTitle: Acoustic noise based permanent magnet flux reduction diagnosis and current compensation in PMSM
abstract: Diagnosis for permanent magnet (PM) flux reduction is necessary for determining motor efficiency. This paper proposes a real-time diagnosis model without invading the motor structure. In this method, acoustic signals acquired with a sound intensity meter under different motor operation conditions are analyzed and processed by a wavelet packet. Moreover, the Grey-Markov Chain model is applied to estimate the flux reduction which is fed to the current compensation algorithm in the vector control drive system. The proposed model is validated in a laboratory designed permanent magnet synchronous motor (PMSM) drive system under different speeds and temperatures.

articleTitle: Point Contact Andreev Reflection and the measurement of spin polarization - towards higher fields and temperatures
abstract: Summary form only given. In this work, PCAR spectra are measured in the standard needle-anvil configuration, where the superconducting tip lands on the film of investigated material, for the case of Nb-Ti. Alternatively, for the case of MgB<sub xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">2</sub>, the superconductor is in thin film form and the investigated material is shaped into a needle, in order to form the point contacts. The conventional low-field and temperature PCAR spectra are interpreted using the modified Blonder-Tinkham-Klapwijk [4] (mBTK) theory allowing for the extraction of a number of fitted parameters superconducting proximity gap (Δ1), barrier strength (Z), spin polarization (P), and effective electronic temperature (Te). The analysis of the high-field and high-temperature PCAR spectra is currently qualitative. The superconducting parameters of both Nb-Ti and MgB<sub xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">2</sub> represent substantial improvement over the traditionally used Nb. The critical temperature of Nb-Ti is 9.5 K, with an upper critical field of about 9 T at 4.2 K, whereas the critical temperature of the MgB<sub xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">2</sub> film is 32.8(8) K, with an upper critical field in excess of 14 T at 4.2 K. Reproducible spin polarization measurements have been possible with Nb-Ti superconducting tips in magnetic fields of up to 7 T.

articleTitle: Tunable permeability and permittivity of low loss NiZnCo ferrite by sintering temperature for VHF-UHF applications
abstract: Summary form only given. In this paper, by modifying the sintering temperature (TS), tunable permeability and permittivity are achieved in NiZnCo ferrite over a wide frequency range. The crystal phase, densification and microstructure of the NiZnCo samples were analyzed to correlate with the variations of the magnetic and dielectric properties. A series of spinel NiZnCo ferrites with nominal composition Ni<sub xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">0.5</sub>Zn<sub xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">0.3</sub>Co<sub xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">0.2</sub>Fe<sub xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">2</sub>O<sub xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">4</sub> were prepared by solid-state reaction method. The samples were sintered in the temperature range of T<sub xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">S</sub>=950°C-1150°C in oxygen gas atmosphere in order to explore the NiZnCo ferrite with matching permeability and permittivity as well as low losses. The phase compositions of the sintering samples were determined by X-ray diffraction (XRD) using Cu Kα radiation at room temperature. The XRD results indicate that all the samples show the formation of single phase cubic spinel structure without any signature of secondary phase. The microstructures of the samples were examined by scanning electron microscope (SEM). It was found that the average grain size and densification were obviously enhanced with increasing sintering temperature. The effects of sintering temperature TS on the magnetic and dielectric properties were systematically investigated. The complex permeability and permittivity spectra, as well as magnetic and dielectric losses of the samples were measured in 10 MHz-1 GHz.

articleTitle: ELF magnetic control of axolotl metamorphosis inspired by administration of thyroid hormone
abstract: In recent studies using amphibious animals, it has been shown that exposures to extremely low frequency (ELF) magnetic fields were able to affect amphibian metamorphosis. The experimental applications utilizing axolotls must be favorable for a direct investigation with respect to aquatic-terrestrial transformations, because the axolotl has been the best understood “neoteny” which refers to a paedomorphosis. The purpose of this study was to investigate the influence of an ELF field on the forced metamorphosis of axolotls, which was induced with the thyroid hormone.

articleTitle: FeCoNi coated glass fabric/polycarbonate composite sheets for electromagnetic absorption and shielding
abstract: The electromagnetic interference (EMI) between the devices and circuits has been widely studied for the noise absorption and the electromagnetic interference suppression of modern electronic devices. Composites with conducting fillers, such as particles, flakes, fibers, fabrics are widely used for EMI shielding. For the metal-polymer composites, the EMI shielding ability can be increased with increasing conductive paths of the filler network. Therefore, we prepared the magnetic materials coated glass fabric (MGF) composite sheets. The magnetic material for coating on glass fabric was employed FeCoNi which has good soft magnetic properties with high magnetic moment. FeCoNi coated on the glass fabric were synthesized by electroless plating process. The polymeric composite sheets were fabricated by using one or two plies of FeCoNi coated glass fabric with or without Ni conductive grids. The Ni grid was placed on both side of FeCoNi coated glass fabric in composite sheet with the total thickness of about 500 mm as shown in Fig. 1. To evaluate the EM characteristics of the laminated composite sheets filled with FeCoNi coated glass fabric, the microwave power absorption and shielding effects were measured by microstrip line (MSL) method up to 10 GHz and shielded loop antenna up to 6 GHz, which is based on IEC 62333 standards. The shielding effectiveness (SE) was measured by using X-band rectangular waveguide (WR90) from 8.2 GHz to 12.4 GHz. We evaluated the shielding behaviors of FeCoNi coated glass fabric composite sheet and insertion effect of conductive Ni grid. The power loss, all of the FeCoNi coated glass fabric composites with or without Ni grid were increased up to 85% at 10 GHz as shown in Fig. 2(a). Inter-decoupling efficiency of the composite sheet filled with 2 layered FeCoNi coated glass fabric and single layer fabric with Ni gird were comparable to that of same thick-Cu foil as shown in Fig. 2(b). SE of single and two layers FeCoNi coated glass fabric in composite exhibited about 50 dB and over 70 dB, respectively. SE of single and two layered FeCoNi coated glass fabric with Ni grid in composite showed over 70 dB as shown in Fig. 2(c). Shielding effect of Ni grid insertion in FeCoNi coated glass fabric composites was comparable to that of Cu foil. The FeCoNi coated glass fabric composite sheet can be a good candidate EMI countermeasure for microwave absorption and shielding in near field and far field region of GHz range.

articleTitle: Efficient nonlinear control of spins by ultrashort THz-fields
abstract: Ultrashort pulses of intense THz radiation have been shown to represent a powerful and versatile tool for spin control. Here, we employ intense THz pulses in two ways to enter the regime of nonlinear THz-spin interaction. In the first approach, we use the magnetic field of intense THz pulses with amplitudes of up to 0.4 T and frequencies between 0.3 and 2 THz to exert a resonant Zeeman torque onto the spins of nickel oxide (NiO). THz-induced magnetic dynamics is monitored by magneto-optical effects that act on the polarization of ultrashort near-infrared laser pulses. In the second approach, we demonstrate this novel concept of spin excitation in the weak ferromagnet thulium orthoferrite (TmFeO<sub xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">3</sub>). In this material, the magnetic anisotropy for the Fe spins is set by electronic orbitals of the Tm ions. THz transients can resonantly excite transitions between these orbital states and thus modify the anisotropy field. We expose a single crystal of TmFeO<sub xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">3</sub> to ultrashort THz pulses of variable peak amplitudes and trace the THz-induced magnetization. The oscillatory magnon traces originate from the quasi-ferromagnetic (q-FM, 0.1 THz) and the quasi-antiferromagnetic (q-AFM, 0.8 THz) mode of TmFeO<sub xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">3</sub>. Surprisingly, the relative strength of the q-FM mode is drastically enhanced when the THz amplitude increases.

articleTitle: Application of Underactuated mechanism motor control in ball and beam system
abstract: Motor control in ball and beam system consists of a beam structure which can be constructed with server electric motor to simulate the Underactuated mechanism system of robot. It can be contacted with a control theory and robot operation in balance behavior. It is well-known that robot structure in 1-D space with a motor to control system balance, which a simple ball and beam system to observe open-loop performance is unstable. When the motor torque and current parameter record from control broad, it will control the beam in balance situation to restrict unstable condition if even it is to be very nearly horizontal. In order to stabilize the ball in beam system, measurement of the ball position and to regulate the beam should be adjusted by the motor device. The control voltage signal goes to the DC motor then the torque generated from the motor drives to regulate the beam to rotate a desired angle. Thus, the ball can be located at the desired position, which is used to simulate the robot behavior system. This study presents a new reduction approach to simplify the type reduction procedure for an interval type-2 fuzzy sliding controller. It should be considered as a collection of a large number type-1 fuzzy set regulated by an interval type-2 fuzzy set. It is shown that a simplified type reduction approach can be used to a hybrid interval type-2 fuzzy sliding controller for a ball-and-beam system. By using the Extended-Karnik-Mendel (EKM) type reduction method, it is indicated that a better results and effectiveness of a hybrid interval type-2 fuzzy sliding controllers, in motor position, torque, current and voltage can be performed a faster position results, at least, reduction of 20%.

articleTitle: Research of magnetocaloric effect of Ni-Mn-In-Co- based Heusler alloys by the direct method in magnetic fields up to 14 T
abstract: Summary form only given. The magnetocaloric effect (MCE) is the adiabatic temperature change (dT<sub xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">ad</sub>) or (and) the isothermal entropy change (dS) of magnet under the influence of a magnetic field. This work is devoted to study of magnetocaloric effect (MCE) in Ni-Mn-In-Co Heusler alloys by direct methods in high magnetic fields. Ni-Mn-In-Co Heusler alloys demonstrate the inverse MCE in the magnetostructural transition area. The adiabatic temperature change value (ΔTad) is determined by direct extraction method in magnetic fields up to 10 T. It is shown that the value of ΔTad increases with decreasing of the difference between the temperature of magnetostructural transition and the Curie point temperatures of the compounds. The amount of isothermal heat emission (sorption) for Ni<sub xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">43</sub>Mn<sub xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">37.8</sub>In<sub xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">12.2</sub>Co<sub xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">7</sub> alloy is determined as a result of magnetization in magnetic field up to 10 T in the magnetostructural transition area. The obtained results are discussed from the viewpoint of magnetic and lattice subsystems influences on the total entropy change (ΔSt).

articleTitle: A correlation analysis of loss density and coil temperature for a motor size design
abstract: This paper presents improved method for analyze correlation of loss density and coil temperature for a motor size design. The conventional method to estimate the temperature of the motor coil considering input current density is limited, because there is due to be the temperature of the motor coil in relation with the calorific value of the volume. The improved method reflects loss of coil, thus, it can increase the prediction accuracy of the coil temperature. In this paper, the conventional method is analyzed to come up with plans to improve it. Above all, the heating and cooling characteristics are made into a numerical formula using the heat equivalent circuit. After then, the loss produced by the coil is divided into the flow channel to the cooling system so that the loss per cooling area can be determined to predict the temperature. The performances of the improved method are analyzed and compared with those of the conventional method. Lastly, the result of the both method are compared with the experimental results to verify the validity of the proposed design process.

articleTitle: Anisotropic consolidation behavior of isotropic Nd-Fe-B HDDR powders during hot deformation
abstract: Summary form only given. In this study, we investigated the anisotropic consolidation behavior of isotropic HDDR powders during hot-deformation. The consolidated Nd-Fe-Ga-Nb-B isotropic magnet was produced from isotropic HDDR powders with a composition of Nd<sub xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">12.5</sub>Fe<sub xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">bal.</sub> Ga<sub xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">0.3</sub>Nb<sub xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">0.2</sub>B<sub xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">6.4</sub> by hot-pressing at 700 °C under 400 MPa in vacuum. Then the isotropic compacts were hot deformed at 700 and 800 °C with deformation rate of ε' = 0.01 and 0.001 s<sup xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">-1</sup> and 40~80 % height reduction. Figure 1 shows the dependence of magnetic properties of die-upsetted magnets produced by various strain rates and processing temperature on strain. The coercivity and remanence of the hot-pressed magnet are 14 kOe and 8 kG, respectively. During the die-upsetting, the coercivity decreased, and remanence increased with increasing strain. The high deformation temperature resulted in a high degree of grain alignment and enhanced remanence. The highest remanence of 13 kG was achieved after die-upsetting with a stain of 1.4 and a strain rate of 0.01 s<sup xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">-1</sup>. Figure 2 shows SEM images of initial HDDR powder and die-upsetted magnet. As shown in Fig. 2 (a), the grain size of the initial HDDR powder is approximately 250 nm, which is similar to single domain size of Nd<sub xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">2</sub>Fe<sub xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">14</sub>B phase, and Nd-rich phase exists along grain boundary. After die-upsetting, the grain morphology is changed from sphere to platelet. It is well known that grains are grown in (010) and (100) orientation into platelet shape and aligned (001) orientation perpendicular to the pressing direction by the interface-controlled solution-precipitation-creep process during die-upset process with melt-spun flakes. The anisotropic consolidation behavior in HDDR powders seems quite similar to that of melt-spun flakes. The grains of die-upsetted magnet are grown from 250 nm to approximately 1 μm. This size is smaller than that of sintered magnet, but lager than that of die-upsetted magnet with melt-spun flakes. However, the die-upsetted magnet with HDDR powders could be subjected to GBDP process at a higher temperature compared with the die-upsetted magnet with melt-spun flakes.

articleTitle: Observation of large planar Hall effect on the current induced spin-orbit effective fields in Ta/MgO/CoFeB/Ta
abstract: Current induced spin-orbit effective magnetic fields in metal/ferromagnet/ oxide trilayer provide an alternative switching mechanism that is more efficient than the conventional spin torque transfer. Perpendicularly magnetised MgO/CoFeB/Ta structures have been widely investigated for logic and non-volatile memories due to its perpendicular magnetic anisotropy and large current induced spin-orbit effective fields.1, 2 However, the understanding of the planar Hall effect of these stacks at low fields are limited. As such, this work evaluates the current dependence of the spin-orbit effective field by considering both the anomalous Hall and planar Hall effect. Harmonic measurements were performed in conjunction with micromagnetic simulations under an in-plane field configuration to affirm the presence of chiral dendritic-like domains, as shown in Figure 1, with and without the application of an in-plane sinusoidal current. Figure 1(c) shows the differential Kerr images of chiral domains, formed due to the presence of Dzyaloshinskii-Moriya interaction (DMI)in the CoFeB/MgO interface. An elongation of the chiral magnetic domains was observed in both measurement configuration such that the elongation direction is perpendicular to the direction of the applied magnetic field. Planar Hall effect contributes significantly to the alteration of the magnetisation state due to lowly tuned anisotropy of CoFeB in both configurations as shown in Figure 1(d). Furthermore, with opposite initial magnetisation states, the second harmonic signals were closely symmetrical about the horizontal axis. As the field was swept and the current was modulated, the second harmonic Hall signals reveal asymmetry and symmetry about the vertical axis for the longitudinal and transverse measurements, respectively. The relationship between the harmonic Hall voltage and the applied magnetic field was used to determine the effective fields through the total energy approach. The results suggest there was a large transverse spin-orbit effective field that arises together with the longitudinal field in the longitudinal measurement. On the other hand, there was larger transverse field than the longitudinal effective field in the transverse measurement. Strong correlations between the modulated current density and large effective fields indicate promising future applications in torque induced logic and memory devices.
